readerTitle: The "almost gone" sign that stopped working
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식당, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 연구 (Worchel, Lee & Adewole 1975 쿠키 항아리 실험)
insight: 희소성과 긴급성은 손님에게 주는 '정보'일 때만 효과가 있다. 그 정보가 거짓이면 효과가 사라지고 신뢰까지 잃는다.
misconception: "마감 임박", "한정 수량"이라고 써 붙이기만 하면 언제나 더 팔린다.

sources.text: Worchel, S., Lee, J., & Adewole, A. (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906–914.
식당과 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Worchel 외(1975) 쿠키 실험: 쿠키 2개가 든 항아리의 쿠키가 10개가 든 항아리의 쿠키보다 더 바람직하다고 평가됨. 10개에서 2개로 줄어든 조건에서 평가가 더 높았다는 내용도 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 효과 크기나 수치를 적지 않았습니다.
이 실험은 소규모 대학생 표본의 오래된 연구입니다. 재현성 논란이 있는지 확인하고, 필요하면 5번 카드 문구를 "one classic study" 수준으로 유지하세요.
7번 카드의 규제 언급은 특정 국가의 법률을 다루지 않도록 "in many places" 수준으로만 적었습니다. 법률 조언처럼 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: The "almost gone" sign that stopped working
body: A neighborhood restaurant added two words to its specials board: *Almost gone!* The first week, the specials sold out early.
The owner kept the words up. Every dish, every night. A month later, specials sold no better than before the sign. Some regulars started joking about it.

image.label: Chalk specials board with 'Almost gone!' next to every dish
image.brief: 식당 입구의 칠판 메뉴판. 모든 메뉴 옆에 똑같은 "Almost gone!" 문구가 반복됨. 앞에 선 단골손님 두 명이 웃으며 눈을 굴리는 모습. 실제 상호나 로고 없음.

cards.title: What goes on tonight's board?
body: You run a small bistro. This morning the chef braised 20 portions of short rib. It takes six hours, so there will be no more tonight.
Which line do you write on the board?

options.text: "Hurry, almost gone!" next to the short rib and the other specials
options.feedback: It creates a rush at first. But when every dish is almost gone, the words stop meaning anything, including the night it is true.

options.text: "Short rib, braised six hours this morning. 20 portions tonight."
options.feedback: It gives a real limit and the reason behind it. Guests learn something true, and the reason doubles as a sign of quality.
Safe and honest, but vague. Guests can't tell if the limit is tonight or next month, so it does little.

cards.title: The sign became wallpaper.
body: Back at the first restaurant, the problem wasn't the words. It was that they never changed.

Regulars saw *Almost gone!* at 6 p.m. and again at 10 p.m. They saw it on dishes that were clearly in stock. So they learned to ignore it. Worse, they started wondering what else on the menu wasn't quite true.
The sign had stopped carrying **information**. Once that happened, it stopped working.

cards.title: Urgency and scarcity
body: **Scarcity** means there's a limited amount. **Urgency** means there's limited time. Both make people act sooner and value the thing more.

Two forces drive this. First, people feel a possible loss more sharply than an equal gain. Missing out hurts. Second, scarcity hints that something is good: *if it's running out, others must want it.*
Both forces depend on the customer believing the limit is real.

cards.title: Two cookies beat ten.
body: In a classic 1975 study, Stephen Worchel and colleagues asked people to taste and rate a cookie. Some took it from a jar holding ten cookies. Others took the same cookie from a jar holding two.
People rated the cookie from the nearly empty jar as more desirable. Same cookie, same taste.
The researchers also found the effect grew when a jar went from ten to two in front of people. A *change* toward scarcity seemed to matter more than scarcity alone.

image.label: Two glass jars: one with ten cookies, one with two
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 똑같은 유리 항아리 두 개. 왼쪽에는 쿠키 10개, 오른쪽에는 쿠키 2개. 오른쪽 항아리 위에 작은 하트나 반짝임 표시로 더 원하게 되는 느낌을 표현. 상표 없음.

cards.title: Real limits come with reasons.
body: Honest scarcity and urgency usually have a cause the customer can understand:
list: **Supply:** a seasonal ingredient, a small batch
**A real date:** an event, a price change, a closing season
cards.callout: Say the limit and the reason. The reason is what makes it believable.

cards.title: Fake limits cost more than they earn.
body: Fake urgency can lift sales once. Then customers learn the pattern and wait it out, or stop trusting your other claims.

Pressure also brings regret. People rushed into buying are more likely to ask for refunds or not come back. And in many places, misleading claims about stock or deadlines can draw attention from consumer regulators.
Even real scarcity has a cost: customers who miss out may feel shut out. Tell them when it comes back.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You sell scheduling software to small clinics. Sign-ups are slow, and the team wants to add urgency to the pricing page. You do plan to raise prices for new customers on March 1.
Which approach do you pick?

options.text: A 15-minute countdown timer on the offer that restarts for each visitor
options.feedback: It may push a few sign-ups. But anyone who reloads the page sees the trick, and clinics buying software for patient data care a lot about trust.

options.text: "Prices for new customers rise on March 1. Sign up before then to keep today's price."
options.feedback: A real date with a clear reason to act. It works because it is true, and it still works when customers check.

options.text: A discount that ends on the last day of every month
options.feedback: Each deadline is technically real. But users soon notice it repeats, so they learn there's no reason to hurry.

cards.title: Scarcity works when it tells the truth.
body: A limit makes people act only if they believe it. State real limits, give the reason, and never use the words when they aren't true.
**Try it today:** find one "limited" or "hurry" message in your business. Write down the real limit behind it. If there isn't one, take it down.
